name: Southern Xiongnu
info: The southern branch of the Xiongnu, formed when eight tribes broke from the chanyu Punu in 48 and settled inside Han China's northern frontier as tributary auxiliaries until Cao Cao ended the chanyu's court.

facts.capital: The southern chanyu's court in Meiji County, Xihe Commandery, from 50; later Pingyang, east of the Fen River in Shanxi
facts.founder: Bi (Pi), the Rizhu King of the Right, acclaimed chanyu in 48
facts.predecessor: The Xiongnu Empire, which split between Punu's Northern Xiongnu and the eight southern tribes
facts.successor: Cao Cao's direct oversight of the Xiongnu of Shanxi, later organised as the Five Divisions

t: In 48 a confederation of eight Xiongnu tribes, with 40,000 to 50,000 men, seceded from the chanyu Punu and acclaimed Bi as chanyu, founding the Southern Xiongnu.
From 50 the Southern Xiongnu were tributaries of Han China, resettled in eight frontier commanderies beside Chinese settlers and reliant on Han trade and annual subsidies.
They served as Han auxiliaries against the Northern Xiongnu, but after rebellions in the 180s the group dissolved, and in 216 Cao Cao detained the chanyu Huchuquan at Ye.
dyk: The Han court often installed southern chanyus who were partial to its interests, and in the late 2nd century the chanyu's own followers killed him for leading them into the Han's internal wars.
ev: Punu ascends the Xiongnu throne in place of Bi, the eldest son of the preceding chanyu, who refuses to attend the annual meeting at court
Eight southern tribes secede from Punu and acclaim Bi as chanyu; their kingdom becomes known as the Southern Xiongnu
The Southern Xiongnu enter tributary relations with Han China, and the chanyu's court is set in Meiji County, Xihe Commandery
The Han general Dou Xian crushes the Northern Xiongnu at the Battle of the Altai Mountains
Rebels among the southern chanyu's followers kill him after he sends his people to fight the Wuhuan for the Han
The chanyu Yufuluo dies at Pingyang and is succeeded by his brother Huchuquan
Cao Cao detains Huchuquan in the city of Ye and sends his uncle Qubei to manage the Xiongnu of Shanxi

sections.foundation:
The Southern Xiongnu grew out of the Xiongnu Empire founded by Modu Chanyu after 209 BCE. In the civil war of 60–53 BCE the chanyu Huhanye moved south and submitted to the Han, using Chinese support against his brother Zhizhi; the Han reduced the Xiongnu from a "brotherly state" to an "outer vassal". Tributary relations lapsed under Huduershi (18–48 CE), who took advantage of the upheavals of the Xin dynasty to regain the Western Regions and at the height of his power compared himself to Modu.

Growing regionalism undid that recovery. Against the principle of fraternal succession set by Huhanye, Huduershi named his son Punu heir. Bi (Pi), the Rizhu King of the Right and eldest son of the preceding chanyu, had the stronger claim and refused to attend the annual meeting at the chanyu's court; in 46 Punu took the throne nonetheless. In 48 a confederation of eight Xiongnu tribes in Bi's power base in the south, with a force of 40,000 to 50,000 men, seceded from Punu and acclaimed Bi as chanyu. This kingdom became known as the Southern Xiongnu, while Punu's rump state around the Orkhon, in north central Mongolia, became the Northern Xiongnu.
sections.socioeconomy:
The Southern Xiongnu were plagued by natural disasters and misfortunes from the start, and in 50 they submitted to tributary relations with Han China. Their people were resettled in eight frontier commanderies, and large numbers of Chinese were settled there at the same time, in mixed Han–Xiongnu settlements. Economically the Southern Xiongnu came to rely on trade with the Han and on annual subsidies from the Chinese court. The poor climate and living conditions of the frontier weighed on them, and many tribesmen left the southern chanyu to return to the steppe and join the Xianbei.

The Xiongnu were a herding people; from their flocks and their horse trade with China their diet is thought to have consisted mainly of mutton, horse meat and wild geese. The Book of Jin names nineteen Xiongnu tribes that resettled within the Great Wall, among them the Chuge, the Qiangqu, the Helai and the Lijie; the Chuge, also called the Xiuchuge, were said to be the most powerful and prestigious. With the fall of the Southern Xiongnu their descendants intermixed with the Han Chinese, Xianbei, Wuhuan and other peoples, and the Xiongnu name gradually disappeared; they were called simply Hu, or formed the core of "mixed Hu" groups.
sections.military:
The Southern Xiongnu served the Han as auxiliaries in defending the northern frontier against nomadic forces. In 49 the Northern Xiongnu were dealt a heavy defeat by the Southern Xiongnu, and the same year the Han governor of Liaodong, Zhai Tong, enticed the Wuhuan and Xianbei to attack the north. The Southern Xiongnu played a role in the defeat of the Northern Xiongnu, who suffered famines from locust plagues, lost their chanyu Youliu to the Xianbei in 87, were crushed by the Han general Dou Xian at the Battle of the Altai Mountains in 89, and after another Han attack in 91 saw their chanyu flee to the north-west.

The victory brought no peace. The surrendered Northern Xiongnu rebelled in 94, dissatisfied with a newly appointed chanyu, and acclaimed Fenghou, who led them beyond the border. The southern tribes now bore the brunt of incessant raids by the rising Xianbei. Those who stayed mutinied from time to time, but failed to gain enough support and were easily put down. In the late 2nd century the southern chanyu sent his people against the Yellow Turban Rebellion and then against the Wuhuan in Hebei in 188. Many Xiongnu feared unending military service to the Han court, and a rebellious faction allied with the Xiuchuge, who had killed the provincial inspector of Bingzhou, and killed the chanyu.
sections.governance:
The Xiongnu were ruled by a chanyu, with the tuqi kings beneath him; the Tuqi King of the Left was normally the heir presumptive. Below them came paired officials of the left and right, the guli, the army commanders, the great governors, the danghu and the gudu, and beneath them the commanders of a thousand, a hundred and ten men, so that the nation was organized like an army. When a chanyu died, power could pass to his younger brother if his son was not of age; this kept an adult on the throne but invited rival claims in later generations, and it was such a dispute that divided the Xiongnu in 48.

As tributaries the Southern Xiongnu came under Han terms first set for Huhanye in 53 BCE: the chanyu or his representatives were to pay homage at the capital, send a hostage prince and present tribute. In 50 the southern chanyu was ordered to set his court in Meiji County, Xihe Commandery. The Chinese court interfered in his politics, often installing chanyus partial to Han interests, and his authority waned as tribesmen left for the steppe. After the chanyu was killed in 188 the Han court named his son Yufuluo, entitled Chizhi Shizhu, but the rebels expelled him; they elected a chanyu of their own and, when he died a year later, left the post vacant under an elderly nominal king.
sections.impact:
The Southern Xiongnu show the limits of what Barfield calls the "inner frontier strategy". In the first Xiongnu civil war, in 60 BCE, the weaker party moved south, submitted to the dominant Chinese regime and used its overlord's resources to defeat its rivals and re-establish the empire. When the Xiongnu divided again around 47 CE the strategy failed: the southern ruler could not defeat the northern one, and the Xiongnu remained divided. The southern tribes nonetheless helped the Han destroy the Northern Xiongnu, most of whom were absorbed by the Xianbei.

Settled inside the frontier, the descendants of the Southern Xiongnu shaped northern China for centuries. In 304 the Five Divisions acclaimed Liu Yuan, who claimed descent from the southern chanyus, though more recent studies suggest he was a Chuge who forged his genealogy; he founded the Han-Zhao state, whose forces sacked Luoyang in 311. Shi Le, founder of the Later Zhao, came from the Qiangqu tribe of the Southern Xiongnu, and the chieftains of the Tiefu, who founded the Helian Xia, descended from Qubei. By the 7th century the Xiongnu had been completely integrated into Chinese society.
sections.decline:
After his expulsion Yufuluo travelled to Luoyang to seek aid, but the Han court was in disorder from the clash between the Grand General He Jin and the eunuchs and the intervention of the warlord Dong Zhuo. He settled with his followers around Pingyang, east of the Fen River in Shanxi, where he died in 195 and was succeeded by his brother Huchuquan. The Southern Xiongnu had effectively dissolved: many of their tribes broke away and kept their distance from the Han civil war, while Yufuluo's group and the Xiuchuge were drawn into it and later subdued by Cao Cao.

The upheaval cost the Han several frontier commanderies of Bing province, among them Shuofang and Yunzhong, which were lost to hostile tribes; Cao Cao abolished them and reduced Bing to the region of modern Shanxi. In 216 he detained Huchuquan in the city of Ye and sent Huchuquan's uncle, Qubei, to manage the remaining Xiongnu vassals in Shanxi. Huchuquan held the title of chanyu in name until his death, after which it was abolished. Brought closer to Chinese rule, the tribes could be watched for rebellion and used as cavalry auxiliaries; they were later divided into the Five Divisions around Taiyuan Commandery, each led by a local chief under the eye of a Chinese resident.

summary: The Southern Xiongnu were the eight Xiongnu tribes that broke away under Bi in 48 and became tributaries of the Han, resettled along the northern frontier and paid to fight the Northern Xiongnu. Weakened by Xianbei raids, Han interference and rebellion, they dissolved in the 190s, and Cao Cao ended their chanyu's court in 216.

pointDescs.48: Eight Xiongnu tribes with 40,000 to 50,000 men secede from Punu and acclaim Bi as chanyu.
pointDescs.49: The Southern Xiongnu deal the Northern Xiongnu a heavy defeat.
pointDescs.50: Beset by natural disasters, the Southern Xiongnu become tributaries of Han China; the chanyu's court is set in Meiji County and his followers are resettled in eight frontier commanderies.
pointDescs.87: The Xianbei defeat the Northern Xiongnu and kill their chanyu Youliu.
pointDescs.89: Dou Xian crushes the Northern Xiongnu at the Battle of the Altai Mountains; the Southern Xiongnu play a role in their defeat.
pointDescs.91: After another Han attack the Northern Chanyu flees to the north-west and those left behind surrender.
pointDescs.94: The surrendered Northern Xiongnu rebel and acclaim Fenghou; Xianbei raids now fall on the southern tribes.
pointDescs.188: The southern chanyu, after sending his people against the Wuhuan, is killed by rebels allied with the Xiuchuge; his son Yufuluo is expelled.
pointDescs.195: Yufuluo dies at Pingyang and is succeeded by Huchuquan; the Southern Xiongnu have effectively dissolved.

notes: The saved article is the general Xiongnu article; the Southern Xiongnu have only a short section of it. The hierarchy, the diet and the lateral succession are told of the Xiongnu in general and are given here as such.
The article names no works in its reference lists (they are empty in the saved text), so references is [].
Barfield's 'inner frontier strategy' is the article's attribution; the article gives only his surname.
The article does not say the Southern Xiongnu fought at the Battle of the Altai Mountains itself, only that they 'played a role in defeating the Northern Xiongnu'; the sections keep to that wording.
The chanyu killed in 188 is not named in the article (the Book of Jin's Qiangqu tribe is named separately).
